title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup

epigraph.quote: The tape is not always right about value, but it is almost always right about timing. A great business in a broken chart is a great business you can buy cheaper later.
epigraph.author: Stan Weinstein, Secrets for Profiting in Bull and Bear Markets (1988), applied to Netweb

web_blocks.html: Every price, moving average, oscillator and support level in this chapter comes from the same-session TradingView snapshot dated 12 November 2026; no technical figure is estimated. At the session close of ₹4,151.90, Netweb's structural position is unambiguous. Price sits below the 50-day simple moving average (₹4,603.33), below the 30-week simple moving average (₹4,548.28) and below the 10-week exponential average (₹4,410.32). It is also fractionally below the 200-day simple moving average (₹4,179.13), by -0.65%. In Stan Weinstein's framework, sustained trade below a declining 30-week moving average defines Stage 4, the declining phase. The deterministic classifier confirms it: Weinstein Stage 4, timing gate CAP_REJECTED.

web_blocks.takeaway: The chart is in Stage 4 with price testing its 200-day shelf and 4-hour momentum ticking up. That combination defines a stabilisation attempt at major support, not a Stage 2 advance; a Stage 2 entry would require first a Stage 1 base and then a decisive breakout back above the 30-week and 50-day averages.

web_blocks.html: The 4-hour timeframe explains why the stock is not in free-fall despite the weak daily and weekly structure. On the 4-hour chart, price has reclaimed its 4-hour EMA20 (₹4,104.43). The 4-hour RSI (49.37) has risen above the daily RSI (43.85). That is a short-term momentum turn consistent with a mean-reversion bounce toward the 50-day average, not the start of a new leg up. The determinant is the 200-day simple moving average at ₹4,179.13: price is sitting almost exactly on it. A weekly close that holds above that shelf, followed by a reclaim of the 30-week average (₹4,548.28), would change the structural classification from Stage 4 toward a Stage 1 basing range. A weekly close below the swing support at ₹3,809.13 would confirm the breakdown and open the ₹3,445 pivot.

One reconciliation is required between two same-session feeds. The market-facts ledger tags Netweb as Stage 1 (Basing), because price is consolidating sideways near a base floor after a long decline. The deterministic Weinstein stage classifier reads Stage 4, because price is trading below a declining 30-week moving average. The two labels describe the same chart; they differ only in which half of the transition they weight. For this dossier the operative classification is Stage 4, because the timing gate keys off the declining 30-week average and price is below it. The reader should treat the Stage 1 (Basing) tag as evidence that a base may be forming, not as evidence that a Stage 2 advance has begun. Note also that two feeds give slightly different oscillator values for the same session — TradingView shows daily RSI 43.85 and ATR ₹210.76, while the market-facts ledger shows RSI 42.47 and ATR ₹213.65. Both readings are neutral, so the divergence does not change the conclusion.

The relative-strength picture is mixed and demands care. Netweb has gained about 18% over the trailing twelve months and 5.4% over six months. But it has lost 16.1% over one month and 20.2% over three months. That is deeply negative momentum versus a benchmark that, per the session ledger, is itself in a narrow-breadth uptrend. The stock's beta to the portfolio is 0.83. Its one-year performance is well behind the AI-cycle leaders like E2E Networks (+87%) and Avalon (+107%). The market has already begun to discriminate within the AI-infrastructure complex. Netweb's own relative strength is no longer a tailwind; it is now a question of whether the recent de-rating has run its course.

Institutional flow tells a similarly cautious story. Promoter holding has fallen from 75.45% at listing to 64.16% by September 2026, a combination of the IPO, the QIP and modest promoter sales. Foreign institutional holding has drifted from a peak above 12% in late 2024 to 9.47% in September 2026. Domestic institutions rose to 7.22% as the QIP brought in local funds. The shareholder count has nearly quadrupled to over 2.6 lakh, which makes the float broad and the stock prone to sentiment swings. There is no evidence in the session ledger of sustained institutional accumulation at current levels. The slight uptick in volume (1.08x the 30-day average) is not the signature of a base being built.

Two levels define the trading thesis. A weekly close below the swing support at ₹3,703.75 invalidates the stabilisation attempt and confirms the Stage 4 decline. Conversely, a weekly close back above the 30-week simple moving average at ₹4,548.28 would be the first credible evidence of a Stage 1 base forming. That breakout would need expanding volume and a daily RSI reclaiming 55 to justify reassessing the entry posture. Between those two lines, the honest stance is patience: there is no Stage 2 momentum edge at the current price.

web_blocks.title: Why the Tape and the Business Diverge
paragraphs: Notice the tension at the centre of this dossier. The business is producing record results — revenue up 335% year-on-year in Q2 FY2027 — while the chart is in Stage 4 and the stock is 28.6% off its high. This is not a contradiction; it is the normal lag between an operating cycle that is still expanding and a share price that had already discounted years of that expansion and is now de-rating as the market questions how long it can last.

For a No-FOMO investor, the divergence is an instruction, not a puzzle. You do not buy a Stage 4 chart simply because the earnings are good, and you do not ignore the earnings simply because the chart is broken. You wait for the two to align — for the price to form a base and break out, or for a genuine support test to offer an asymmetric entry. That alignment is what the final chapter resolves.

book_paragraphs: Let us read the tape together, because in a fast, cyclical stock like Netweb the chart is not a decoration — it is a risk-management tool. Every number in this chapter is from the same 12 November 2026 session, so we are looking at the same picture. The close was ₹4,151.90, and if you plot it against the moving averages the story is stark: the stock is below its 50-day average (₹4,603), below its 30-week average (₹4,548), below its 10-week average (₹4,410), and just barely below its 200-day average (₹4,179) — by 0.65%.

In Stan Weinstein's vocabulary, sustained trade below a declining 30-week moving average is Stage 4, the declining phase, and that is exactly where Netweb sits. The deterministic classifier agrees: Stage 4, and the timing gate reads CAP_REJECTED, meaning new positions should not be initiated into this structure. If you have internalised only one rule of this whole philosophy, let it be this: you do not catch a falling knife, no matter how good the business is, because a better price almost always comes.

But look more carefully, because the tape is not uniformly bearish. On the 4-hour chart, price has clawed back above its 4-hour EMA20 and 4-hour RSI (49.37) has edged above the daily RSI of 43.85. That is the signature of a short-term bounce attempt, not a trend reversal. And the stock is sitting almost precisely on its 200-day moving average, the last major structural shelf — a level that has historically been where a de-rating either stops or accelerates. Watch that shelf, and watch the swing support at ₹3,809. Above, the first real test is the 30-week average at ₹4,548, then the 50-day at ₹4,603.

The momentum readings across timeframes tell a coherent story. Daily RSI is 43.85, weekly 45.57, 4-hour 49.37 — all neutral, none oversold, none overbought. This is not capitulation; it is a grind. Daily ATR is ₹210.76, about 5% of the price, which tells you exactly how much the stock can move in a day and therefore how large a position you can responsibly carry. And the Bollinger-band width of 27% says the base is still wide and volatile, not coiled and quiet — a real Stage 1 base would show contracting volatility, and we do not have it yet.

Now bring in the context that matters most for a stock — how it behaves relative to its peers. Netweb has gained about 18% over the past year, but it has lost 16% in the past month and 20% in the past three. Compare that with E2E Networks (+87% over a year) and Avalon Technologies (+107%): the market has begun to discriminate inside the AI-infrastructure complex, and Netweb is on the wrong side of that discrimination right now. Its relative strength, once a tailwind, has become a headwind. Meanwhile the institutional picture is one of diffusion rather than conviction: promoter holding down to 64.16%, FIIs down to 9.47%, the shareholder count nearly quadrupled. There is no evidence in the session data of the quiet accumulation that marks a genuine base.

So why does the tape look so different from the business? Because the price had already discounted years of growth, and it is now marking that expectation down as the market asks how long the AI capex wave runs. The business is still compounding; the multiple was just too high. This divergence is not confusion — it is information. It tells you that the market has moved from pricing Netweb as an AI proxy to pricing it as a cyclical integrator with a great order book and an uncertain endgame.

For you, the divergence is an instruction. Do not buy a Stage 4 chart merely because the earnings are exciting, and do not dismiss the earnings merely because the chart is broken. Wait for the two to agree — for the price either to fall into its support shelf and hold, offering an asymmetric entry, or to build a genuine base and break back above the 30-week average. Until then, the tape is telling you the same thing the valuation chapter did: there is a great business here, and there is no hurry to own it at this price.

Think of the chart, finally, as the market's running vote on everything the earlier chapters established. When the tape was strong in 2024 and 2025, the market was voting that Netweb's integration moat and order book were durable and worth a premium. When it fell 28% from August 2026, the market was not voting that the business broke; it was voting that the price had gotten ahead of the evidence, and that the cash-conversion and customer-concentration questions were now part of the value. This is why you and I read the tape after the fundamentals, not instead of them. The chart tells you what the crowd currently believes, and your job is to decide whether the crowd is early, right, or late. On the current evidence, the crowd is early in its caution, which means your edge is patience rather than courage.

book_callouts.title: The 200-Day Line in the Sand
book_callouts.text: Notice that Netweb is sitting within 1% of its 200-day moving average while still well below its 30-week and 50-day averages. That configuration — a long-term support shelf being tested from above a broken medium-term trend — is where de-ratings often pause or pivot. It is the single most important level to watch in the next few weeks. A weekly close below ₹3,809 turns the pause into a breakdown; a reclaim of ₹4,548 begins the repair.
